Write the explainer section for a database internals guide, for a developer deciding whether to put a Bloom filter in front of a slow lookup. The question it answers: What is a Bloom filter, and when is it worth putting in front of a slow lookup?

Facts, each checked against the original paper and the LevelDB source:

- A Bloom filter is a fixed-size array of bits plus k hash functions. It answers whether a key is in a set.
- Adding a key sets the k bits its hashes point to.

- The best k for a given array size and key count is bits per key times ln 2.
- A filter cannot remove a key, because clearing a bit could erase another key that shares it.
- A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter so that keys can be removed.
- A filter cannot list its keys or return a value.
- LevelDB keeps one filter per file on disk, so a read skips every file whose filter says no.

graders.evidence:
## Bloom filters

A Bloom filter answers one question about a set of keys: has this key been added? It sits in front of a slow lookup, such as a read from disk, and answers most lookups for absent keys before the slow work starts.

The filter is a fixed-size array of bits, all 0 at first, and k hash functions. Adding a key hashes it k ways and sets the k bits the hashes point to. Checking a key hashes it the same way and reads those k bits. If any of them is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set that bit. If all are 1, the key probably was added, but other keys may have set the same bits. The filter therefore never gives a false negative, and it can give a false positive.

Every added key sets more bits, so the false positive rate rises as the array fills. With about 10 bits per key and 7 hashes the rate is near 1%. For a given array size and key count, the best k is bits per key times ln 2, which is where 7 comes from at 10 bits per key. Running k separate hash functions is unnecessary, because double hashing derives all k bit positions from two hash values, so the filter needs only two real hash functions.

The filter stores bits and no keys, which limits what it can do. It cannot list its keys or return a value. It cannot remove a key either, because clearing a bit could erase another key that shares it. A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter, so adding a key increments its k counters and removing it decrements them.

A filter pays off when the lookup behind it is slow and many lookups ask for keys that are not there. A "no" costs k bit reads and ends the lookup. A "yes", true or false, still runs the full lookup, which also fetches the value the filter cannot supply. At a 1% false positive rate, about 99 of every 100 lookups for absent keys stop at the filter. When nearly every lookup finds its key, the filter answers yes each time and only adds work.

LevelDB uses the filter this way. It keeps one filter per file on disk, so a read skips every file whose filter says no and reads only the files that might hold the key.

## What is a Bloom filter?

A Bloom filter is a fixed-size array of bits plus k hash functions, and it answers one question: is this key in the set? A check is cheap, so the filter can sit in front of a slow lookup and answer "no" without the lookup ever running.

Adding a key runs it through the k hash functions and sets the k bits they point to. Checking a key computes the same k positions and reads them. If any of those bits is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set that bit. If all are 1, the key probably was added. The word "probably" is there because other keys may have set the same bits. The filter therefore never gives a false negative, but it can give a false positive.

The false positive rate rises as the array fills, because more bits are 1 and a key that was never added is more likely to find all k of its bits already set. With about 10 bits per key and 7 hashes the rate is near 1%. For a given array size and key count, the best k is bits per key times ln 2, which is where 7 comes from at 10 bits per key. The k positions do not need k independent hash functions. Double hashing derives all of them from two hash values, so the filter needs two real hash functions.

A filter cannot remove a key, because clearing a bit could erase another key that shares it. A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter that goes up on add and down on remove, so keys can be removed, and each slot takes more space than a bit. A filter also cannot list its keys or return a value. It says yes or no, so it goes in front of a lookup and does not replace one.

A filter saves work only on a "no", so it pays when many of the lookups are for keys that are absent. A "yes" still runs the full lookup, and a false positive adds one lookup that finds nothing. LevelDB keeps one filter per file on disk, so a read skips every file whose filter says no and opens only the files that might hold the key.

## What a Bloom filter is, and when it is worth putting in front of a slow lookup

A Bloom filter is a small, fixed-size structure that answers one question about a set of keys: has this key been added? It is cheap to check and small enough to keep in memory, so it can sit in front of a slow lookup, such as a read from disk, and rule out the lookups that would find nothing.

The filter is an array of bits, all starting at 0, plus k hash functions. To add a key, the filter runs it through each hash function and sets the k bits they point to. To check a key, it reads those same k bits. If any of them is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set all k. If all of them are 1, the key probably was added.

The "probably" comes from sharing. Other keys may have set the same positions, so a key that was never added can find all of its bits already set, which is a false positive. The reverse cannot happen. An added key keeps its bits set, so the filter never gives a false negative. A "no" is therefore certain, and a "yes" is a hint that the real lookup still has to confirm.

How often the hint is wrong depends on how full the array is. Every added key sets more bits, so the false positive rate rises as the array fills. With about 10 bits per key and 7 hashes, the rate is near 1%. For a given array size and key count, the best number of hashes is bits per key times ln 2, which is where 7 comes from at 10 bits per key. Running seven independent hash functions per key would be costly, so implementations use double hashing, which derives all k positions from two hash values and needs only two real hash functions.

The structure has hard limits. It cannot remove a key, because clearing a bit could erase another key that shares it. A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter, incrementing on add and decrementing on remove, so that keys can be deleted. The filter also cannot list the keys it holds or return a value for one. It says yes or no and nothing more.

These properties decide when a filter pays for itself. It helps when a lookup has several places it could look and the key is in few of them, because each certain "no" skips a slow lookup. LevelDB works this way. It keeps one filter per file on disk, and a read skips every file whose filter says no. The cost is memory, about 10 bits per key for a 1% false positive rate, plus the lookups that false positives still send through. A filter does nothing for a key that is usually present, since the slow lookup has to run anyway, and it cannot replace the lookup when the caller needs the value.

cases.name: writing-prose-go-defer
cases.promptMarkdown:
Write the explainer section for a Go language guide, for a developer about to use defer to release resources. The question it answers: When does a deferred call run in Go, for someone using defer to release a resource?

Facts, each checked against the Go specification:

- `defer` schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, not at the end of the enclosing block.
- The arguments of the deferred call are evaluated when the `defer` statement runs, not when the call runs.
- For a method call, the receiver is evaluated when the `defer` statement runs too.
- Deferred calls run last in, first out.
- Deferred calls also run when the function panics.
- A deferred function literal can read and set the function's named results.
- In a loop each iteration adds a deferred call, and none run until the function returns, so `defer f.Close()` in a loop keeps every file open until then.
- A deferred call of a nil function value panics when the call runs, not at the `defer` statement.
- Since Go 1.14 the compiler inlines most defers at function exit, so a defer costs a few nanoseconds.

cases.name: writing-prose-groupcache
cases.promptMarkdown:
Write the explainer section for the groupcache README, for a developer deciding whether to use groupcache. The question it answers: How does groupcache work, for someone deciding whether to use it?

Facts, each checked against the code:

- groupcache is a Go library for caching across a cluster of processes.
- Every process holds part of the cache and serves it to the others, so there are no cache servers.
- Peers are given to a process through `SetPeers()`.
- Keys sit on a consistent hash ring. A process finds a key's owner by hashing against its own copy of the ring, with no network call.
- Each key has one owner.
- `Get()` checks the main cache (keys the process owns) and the hot cache (copies of keys peers own) first, then asks the owner.
- The owner runs the `Getter` and passes the value back through a `Sink`.
- The hot cache is bounded relative to the main cache, so copies of peer-owned keys cannot take over the keys the process owns.
- When a peer joins or leaves, only the keys on its part of the ring change owner.
- Singleflight allows one in-flight load per key. A million `Get("FOO")` calls run the `Getter` once.
- If the owner is unreachable, the asking process runs the `Getter` itself, so the `Getter` can run on more than one process.
- `Set()`, `Remove()` and `RemoveKeys()` go to the owner and then to every other peer, best effort, so values should carry an expiry.
- The default cache is an LRU. The Otter cache uses lock-free S3-FIFO eviction.
- HTTP is the default transport.
- Stats are OpenTelemetry metrics.
- There is no global state.

## How groupcache works

groupcache is a Go library for caching across a cluster of processes. Every process holds part of the cache and serves it to the others, so there are no cache servers to run. Each process learns who its peers are through `SetPeers()`.

Keys sit on a consistent hash ring, and every process keeps its own copy of the ring. A process finds the owner of a key by hashing it against that copy, which gives each key exactly one owner. `Get()` first checks the main cache, which holds the keys the process owns, and the hot cache, which holds copies of keys that peers own. On a miss it asks the owner. The owner runs the `Getter` you supplied to load the value from its source, and passes the value back through a `Sink`. The hot cache is bounded relative to the main cache, so copies of peer-owned keys cannot take over the space for the keys the process owns.

Concurrent requests for one key share a single load, because singleflight allows one in-flight load per key. A million `Get("FOO")` calls run the `Getter` once. Adding or removing a peer changes the owner of the keys on that peer's part of the ring, and every other key keeps its owner.

Two behaviours matter when deciding whether groupcache fits. If the owner is unreachable, the asking process runs the `Getter` itself, so the `Getter` can run on more than one process at a time and has to tolerate that. And `Set()`, `Remove()` and `RemoveKeys()` go to the owner and then to every other peer on a best-effort basis, so a peer can miss an update. Values should carry an expiry so a stale copy ages out.

The default cache evicts in LRU order, and the Otter cache evicts with a lock-free S3-FIFO. Peers talk over HTTP by default, stats are reported as OpenTelemetry metrics, and groupcache keeps no global state.

## How groupcache works

groupcache is a Go library for caching across a cluster of processes. Every process holds part of the cache and serves it to the others, so a deployment has no cache servers to run. The application tells each process who its peers are by calling `SetPeers()`, and the processes handle the rest among themselves.

Keys are placed on a consistent hash ring, and each key has exactly one owner. A process hashes a key against its own copy of the ring to find that owner. `Get()` looks in two local caches first: the main cache, which holds the keys this process owns, and the hot cache, which holds copies of keys that peers own. On a miss in both, it asks the owner. The owner runs your `Getter`, the function that loads the value from its real source, and hands the result back through a `Sink`. The hot cache is bounded relative to the main cache, so copies of popular peer-owned keys cannot crowd out the keys the process owns.

Loads are collapsed by singleflight, which allows one in-flight load per key, so a million `Get("FOO")` calls run the `Getter` once. Because ownership comes from the ring, a peer that joins or leaves moves the keys on its part of the ring to new owners, and the rest of the keys stay where they were.

Three behaviours matter when deciding whether groupcache fits. First, if the owner is unreachable, the asking process runs the `Getter` itself, so the `Getter` can run on more than one process and must be safe to do so. Second, `Set()`, `Remove()` and `RemoveKeys()` go to the owner and then to every other peer on a best-effort basis. A peer that misses an update keeps its old copy, so values should carry an expiry. Third, the default cache evicts with an LRU, and the Otter cache is available for lock-free S3-FIFO eviction.

HTTP is the default transport between peers. Stats are reported as OpenTelemetry metrics, and the library keeps no global state.

cases.name: writing-prose-write-ahead-log
cases.promptMarkdown:
Write the explainer section for a database internals guide, for a developer who has not seen how databases survive a crash. The question it answers: How does a write-ahead log keep a database from losing committed data in a crash?

Facts, each checked against the Postgres documentation:

- A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change.
- The database changes data pages in memory and writes them to disk later.
- Before it changes a page, it appends a record describing the change to the log.
- A transaction commits when its records and a commit record have been flushed to disk with fsync. The data pages do not have to be.
- Appending to the end of a file is sequential, so flushing the log costs much less than flushing pages scattered across the data files.
- After a crash the database replays the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies each record to its page.
- Every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it, so replay skips records a page already has.
- A checkpoint writes all modified pages to disk and notes the log position. The log before it can be deleted or reused.
- Postgres calls this the WAL, and replicas stay current by replaying the same records.
- Postgres stores the log in 16 MB segment files by default.
- In Postgres an LSN is a byte position in the log.

graders.evidence:
## How a write-ahead log survives a crash

A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change. It exists so that a crash cannot take away data the database has already told a client is committed.

The database changes data pages in memory and writes them to disk later, so a crash can lose any page that has not been written yet. To cover that, the database appends a record describing the change to the log before it changes the page. The page may vanish with memory, but the record of the change is already in the file.

Commit depends on this. A transaction commits when its records and a commit record have been flushed to disk with fsync, which makes the operating system put the data on the disk before returning. The data pages do not have to be flushed. This is also the cheaper choice, because the log is only ever appended to at its end, which is sequential, while the pages a transaction changed are scattered across the data files and flushing them would cost much more.

After a crash, the database replays the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies each record to its page. Some of those pages reached disk before the crash and already contain the change, so every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it. Replay compares the two and skips any record the page already has. In Postgres, an LSN is a byte position in the log.

A checkpoint is what keeps replay short. It writes all modified pages to disk and notes the position in the log, so everything before that position is already in the data files. The log before it can be deleted or reused, and recovery only has to replay what came after it.

Postgres calls this log the WAL and stores it in 16 MB segment files by default.

## How a write-ahead log keeps committed data through a crash

A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change. It exists so that a transaction the database has reported as committed survives a crash, even when the pages that hold its changes were still only in memory.

The database does not write a page to disk each time it changes one. It changes the page in memory and writes it out later. Before it changes the page, it appends a record describing the change to the log. A transaction commits when its records and a commit record have been flushed to disk with fsync, and the data pages do not have to be. When the flush returns, everything needed to redo the transaction is on disk, and the database can report the commit.

Flushing the log costs much less than flushing the pages. Appending to the end of a file is sequential, while the modified pages are scattered across the data files. A commit therefore waits for one sequential flush, and the scattered page writes happen later.

A crash loses the contents of memory, so some committed changes exist only in the log. To recover, the database replays the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies each record to its page. Every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it. Some pages were written to disk before the crash and already hold some of the changes, so replay compares the two numbers and skips any record the page already has. A page that was written before the crash receives only the records it is missing.

A checkpoint is what keeps replay short. It writes all modified pages to disk and notes the current position in the log. Everything before that position is already in the data files, so replay starts there, and the log before it can be deleted or reused.

Postgres calls this log the WAL and stores it in segment files of 16 MB by default. A Postgres LSN is a byte position in the log. Replicas stay current by replaying the same records the primary wrote, which is the replay a primary performs after a crash.

graders.evidence:
## How a write-ahead log survives a crash

A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change. It lets a transaction commit without writing every page it modified to disk, and still survive a crash. Postgres calls it the WAL.

The database changes data pages in memory and writes them to disk later, so a crash can destroy changes that were never written to their pages. To keep them, the database appends a record describing each change to the log before it changes the page. A transaction commits when its records and a commit record have been flushed to disk with fsync, which forces the data out of the operating system's cache and onto the disk. The data pages do not have to be flushed at that point.

Flushing only the log is what makes commits fast. Appending to the end of a file is sequential, so it costs much less than flushing the pages a transaction touched, which are scattered across the data files.

After a crash the memory is empty, and some committed changes exist only in the log. The database replays the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies each record to its page. Every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it. Replay compares the two and skips a record when the page already has it, so a page that reached the disk before the crash is not changed a second time. In Postgres an LSN is a byte position in the log.

A checkpoint is what keeps replay short. It writes all modified pages to disk and notes the current position in the log, and the log before that position is no longer needed for recovery, so it can be deleted or reused. Replay starts from the last checkpoint for the same reason.

Because the log is a complete, ordered record of changes, it has a second use in Postgres: replicas stay current by replaying the same records.
